text.p: Volkswagen AG, the world's fourth-largest carmaker, powered ahead in the first half of 1997 as group net profit surged 73 percent to 488 million marks despite a rise of 12 percent in sales.
VW increased the amount of money it earned per vehicle sold in the six-month period as group sales rose at a sharply faster pace than the growth in vehicle output, sales and deliveries to customers.
VW, which sells vehicles under the VW, Skoda, SEAT and Audi brands, said group net profit rose to 488 million marks from 282 million in the 1996 period.
Group sales, getting a boost from the weak mark helping exports, rose to 56.55 billion marks from 50.5 billion.
VW predicted it would report higher profits for all of 1997 compared with 1996, when it had a net profit of 678 billion marks on sales of 100.1 billion.

Despite weakening sales at home, blamed in part on the upcoming model changeover for the popular Golf, VW said global vehicle sales rose nine percent to 2.185 million units from 2.015 million in the 1996 period.

In the fiercely competitive west European market, VW said its sales outside Germany rose nearly eight percent to 782,818 vehicles and boosted its market share, including Germany, to 17.6 percent from 17.3 percent.
Production in the VW group rose to 2.207 million vehicles, up eight percent from 2.040 million, while vehicle deliveries rose 10 percent to 2.194 million units from 1.996 million.

But VW continued to have troubles in the German market, where it said sales in the six-month period fell to 511,088 vehicles from 515,142 in the 1996 period. Its dominant German market share slipped to 27.1 percent from 27.3 percent.
While 1996 sales rose 11 percent to 3.99 million vehicles, VW's domestic sales rose only 2.3 percent to 958,522 vehicles.

One reason cited by industry analysts for the weak sales has been that potential buyers were waiting for the launch of the new model of the Golf, upon which VW depends for about half of its global sales, this autumn at the Frankfurt car show.
Still, industry analysts said the results showed the carmaker's recovery launched by VW chief executive Ferdinand Piech in 1993 was clearly showing results.
They also noted that VW boosted its workforce by four percent to 270,211 workers, in an effort to help cut delivery times that have risen sharply due to high demand for almost all key models.
"The momentum at VW is still improving and that was particularly evident in the second quarter," said Andrew Blair-Smith, an analyst at BZW in Frankfurt.
"The recovery should accelerate a bit in the second half and net profit should be up about 70 percent for the year, or in line with the pace seen in the first half," he said.
VW saw particular strength in sales from its Czech-made Skoda brand, which recorded a gain of 27 percent to 161,888 vehicles in the six-month period.

Volkswagen brand sales rose 10 percent to 1.557 million units, while sales of luxury market segment Audi cars rose nearly 13 percent to 276,073 vehicles. At SEAT in Spain, sales rose about eight percent to 198,590 vehicles.
"An important point is the general improvement in sales across the group," said Christian Obst, analyst at Vereinsbank in Munich. "They are moving in the right direction."
VW said North American sales rose 14.6 percent to 129,479 vehicles, which included a five percent rise in the United States to 69,299 and a 33 percent rise in Mexico to 28,931.
The region's sales were helped in particular by Audi, which reported a 34 percent rise in U.S. sales to 17,019 vehicles.
In Brazil, where VW is investing in new production plants, the carmaker said sales rose 18.5 percent to 321,199 vehicles and its top market share position stayed at 35 percent.
